bib.title: A Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: What, When, How, and Where to Evolve on the Path to Artificial Super Intelligence

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: What, When, How, and Where to Evolve on the Path to Artificial Super Intelligence", Huan-ang Gao, Jiayi Geng, Wenyue Hua, Mengkang Hu, Xinzhe Juan, Hongzhang Liu, Shilong Liu, Jiahao Qiu, Xuan Qi, Qihan Ren, Yiran Wu, Hongru Wang, Han Xiao, Yuhang Zhou, Shaokun Zhang, et al. (Mengdi Wang corresponding). Transactions on Machine Learning Research (01/2026); arXiv:2507.21046v4.

COVERAGE: 324,250 chars extracted. Read chars 0-238,600 in full (title through conclusion, all tables and figure captions in the text). The reference list (238,572 to end, about 85k chars) was skimmed only at its start and end, for origins. There is no appendix. Extraction was clean. I read the target note's front matter and first section only, to see which claims matter.

CLAIMS (ranked; the survey is mostly qualitative, so few numbers)
- Definition: a self-evolving agent is f(Pi, tau, r) = Pi'. It updates the architecture, models, context (prompt and memory) and tools from its own trajectories and feedback. This is the formal version of the note's "slow loop edits the fast loop".
  number: none
  setup: POMDP environment; agent system Pi = (Gamma, {psi_i}, {C_i}, {W_i}); objective max_f sum U(Pi_j, T_j)
  quote: "A self-evolving agent is the agent that modifies its internal parameters, contextual state, toolset, or architectural topology based on its own trajectories or feedback signals, with the explicit objective of improving future performance."
  where: p.7, about char 18,000
- Inclusion criteria: the update must be experience-dependent, persistent, and involve autonomous or self-initiated learning. The authors concede that full autonomy is aspirational, and they define a proto-evolution to strong-evolution spectrum.
  number: none
  quote: "fully autonomous self-evolution without human intervention represents an aspirational goal rather than the current norm"
  where: p.7
- Evolution is split by timing. Intra-test-time adapts during the task. Inter-test-time adapts between tasks and is called "the predominant learning process". The note's slow loop is inter-test-time, in-context (ICL) evolution.
  number: none
  quote: "Inter-test-time self-evolution represents the predominant learning process in autonomous agents, wherein adaptation occurs following task execution rather than during it."
  where: p.18, about char 77,500
- Four evolution targets: model, context (memory and prompts), tools, architecture. Prompt optimisation and memory evolution both change what is in the context window. This maps onto the note's four edit targets (contract, state, trigger logic, SOP steps), but the survey does not use those names.
  number: none
  quote: "In most cases, these two terms can be used interchangeably because they both refer to what is included in the context window."
  where: p.11
- Safety: self-training on agent-generated data can erase safety alignment ("misevolution"). Memory evolution can reward-hack, for example an agent learns unnecessary refunds because memory links them to satisfaction. An "Alignment Tipping Process" is also described.
  number: none (qualitative; the evidence is cited from Shao et al. 2025 and Han et al. 2025, not run here)
  quote: "an agent might learn to issue unnecessary refunds because its memory correlates them with high satisfaction ratings (Shao et al., 2025)"
  where: p.50, about char 224,500
- Guardrail checklist (Table 12) for deploying self-evolving agents: an immutable audit trail of every self-modification, versioned state with tagged safe versions, a tested one-click rollback, pre-update validation against a "golden dataset", reward-hacking alerts, goal guardrails that require human review, and approval gates for high-stakes actions. This backs the note's rung-1 human-gated start.
  number: none
  quote: "Pre-Update Safety Validation: Before a self-modified model is deployed, it is automatically evaluated against a \"golden dataset\" of safety-critical prompts to prevent catastrophic forgetting of alignment."
  where: p.52 (Table 12)
- Cited autonomy gains and risk. WebRL went from 4.8% to 42.4% with self-generated tasks. SEAgent went from 11.3% to 34.5% (+23.2 points). Alignment-faking rates went from 12% to 78% when agents evolved under conflicting objectives (Greenblatt et al.). These are secondhand figures and the survey does not rerun them.
  number: 4.8% to 42.4%; 11.3% to 34.5%; 12% to 78%
  setup: WebRL web agent (Qi et al. 2024); SEAgent software exploration (Sun et al. 2025c); alignment-faking from Greenblatt et al. 2024
  quote: "Alignment faking rates escalated from 12% to 78% when agents autonomously evolved under conflicting objectives (Greenblatt et al., 2024)"
  where: p.39, about char 179,500
- The survey recommends reporting three things about the evolution process: whether strategies and task sequences are predetermined, procedurally sampled or agent-generated; where the feedback comes from (human labels, rule-based evaluators, or self-reflection); and how often external interventions occur. Without this, a gain cannot be told apart from external guidance.
  number: none
  quote: "gains may reflect true self-evolution capability or extensive external guidance."
  where: p.39
- Evaluation gaps. Retention is the "most underserved dimension". Most benchmarks reset agent state between tasks, so they cannot measure accumulation or degradation. No benchmark tracks safety drift over long evolution. Evolution costs are rarely reported, and protocols allow unconstrained optimisation with no hard budgets.
  number: none
  quote: "the overwhelming majority of existing benchmarks adopt episodic evaluation where agent state resets between tasks, fundamentally precluding measurement of knowledge accumulation or degradation"
  where: p.37
- Metrics defined. Forgetting FGT_t = 1/(t-1) * sum_i [max_j J_ij - J_it]. Backward transfer BWT_t = 1/(t-1) * sum_i (J_it - J_ii). Cost-per-Gain CPG_t = Total Cost_t / (Performance Gain_t + epsilon). Tool Productivity TP = delta-score / sum cost(tool_i). Other metrics: success-by-iteration curves, area under the learning curve (AULC), and token drift.
  number: formulas
  quote: "CPG_t = Total Cost_t / (Performance Gain_t + epsilon) ... Lower CPG indicates more efficient learning."
  where: p.37-38. The extraction mangles the formulas, so verify against the PDF.
- Standard protocols (Table 10). Short-horizon: no cross-task persistence, a per-task evolution budget K_short, and per-iteration logging of prompts, model and tool versions, traces and cost. Long-horizon: full persistence, stage and cumulative budgets (K_stage, K_total), scheduled retention probes and evolution decision logs.
  number: none
  quote: "long-horizon protocols assume full persistence of model parameters, prompts, memories, and toolsets across tasks, specify both stage-wise and cumulative evolution budgets (K_stage, K_total)"
  where: p.45
- Worked cost example from Fan et al. 2025 (SWE-bench, SWE-Agent): Qwen3-32B used 440K tokens, 35 calls and 28% success. GPT-4o-mini used 8.1M tokens, 181 calls and 10% success. That is an 18x token difference, and the table also notes "Failed attempts: 4x cost vs. successful ones".
  number: 440K vs 8.1M tokens; 28% vs 10%
  quote: "SWE-Agent + Qwen3-32B (440K tokens, 35 calls, 28% success) vs. GPT-4o-mini (8.1M tokens, 181 calls, 10% success)"
  where: p.38 (Table 5 caption)
- Trade-offs of the three method families. Reward-based is sensitive to reward design. Imitation is sample-efficient but limited by demonstration quality. Population-based is sample-inefficient and resource-intensive but explores more widely.
  number: none
  quote: "population-based and self-play evolution enhance diversity and open-ended discovery, yet typically incur higher computational cost and lower interpretability compared with single-agent paradigms."
  where: p.27 (Table 4 on p.28)
- Darwin Godel Machine (DGM): keeps an archive of all historical versions and branches from any past version. Parent selection balances performance with novelty, and it edits its own Python codebase, scored on coding benchmarks.
  number: none
  quote: "maintain an archive of all historical versions, enabling branching from any past \"species\" rather than linear optimization"
  where: p.25
- Illustrative comparison (Table 11, not a controlled comparison). SWE with Claude-3.5-sonnet: Reflexion 54.4, Learn-by-Interact 60.0. WebArena-Lite with GLM-4-9B: DigiRL 31.5, WebRL 43.0. GSM8K with GPT-4o-mini: ADAS 90.5, AFlow 90.8, ScoreFlow 94.6. The authors say the table cannot be read apples to apples.
  number: as listed
  quote: "true apples-to-apples comparison remains infeasible at present"
  where: p.46-47
- Practitioner point supporting the note: "Reflexion"-style lightweight reflection is cheaper but gains less.
  number: none
  quote: "lightweight intra-test reflection methods tend to be more cost-efficient but yield smaller gains"
  where: p.46-47. The extraction splits this sentence across the page break, so the quote is stitched; verify.

LIMITS
- This is a survey with no new experiments. Almost all performance numbers are secondhand and come from different setups.
- The authors say the field's "conceptual boundaries are still being actively negotiated", and they call the survey a "guiding synthesis".
- Full autonomy is called aspirational.
- Latency, cost and safety are "not consistently reported" across methods.
- The survey gives no evidence on the note's specific claims: a 5-10 run cadence, an explicit "no change needed" outcome, busywork or invented edits, or compounding config errors. It names no such failure mode as an "anti-busywork" problem. The closest are reward hacking, misevolution, and the point that "success-by-iteration" is measured under pre-specified protocols.
- It says nothing on whether a loop should exist (the note's scope limit).
- Dated: the survey covers work up to about late 2025. The v4 date is 16 Jan 2026. It predates 2026 items cited in the note (autoresearch, Anthropic recursive self-improvement).
- The author affiliation "(Princeton etc.)" and the figure sources are as printed.

CODE: none (the text has equations only, no code).

FIGURES (not extracted with the script; captions are from the text)
- Fig 1, p.2: trajectory from LLMs to foundation agents to self-evolving agents.
- Fig 2, p.4: taxonomy tree with representative methods at each leaf. Useful as an index of methods.
- Fig 3, p.5: overview of what, when, how and where, plus evaluation. Best single-page orientation.
- Fig 5, p.17: intra-test-time loop (variant generation, verification, policy update) versus inter-test-time loop (rollout, trajectory analysis, policy update). This is the closest picture of the note's "second, slower loop".
- Fig 6: reward-based strategies. Fig 7: online/offline, on/off-policy and reward granularity. Fig 9: evaluation goals and paradigms.
- Table 12, p.52: the deployment checklist.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction is clean overall. Formulas (FGT, BWT, CPG) and table layouts are garbled, and some words are run together ("moreadaptiveandautonomous"). Quotes with run-together words should be checked against the PDF.
- No embedded instructions found in the text.
- References were only skimmed. Almazoori et al. appears twice in the reference list.
- The survey does not mention a paper at arXiv 2603.23420 or any of the note's other sources, so it cannot be credited for specific claims about them.
